```{r setup}
#| include: false
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, comment = "#>", 
                      fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 5, fig.fullwidth=TRUE,
                      fig.align = "center", out.height="auto")
options(knitr.kable.NA = "")

bayesplot::bayesplot_theme_set(ggplot2::theme_gray())
bayesplot::color_scheme_set(scheme = "brightblue")

library(housepi)
set.seed(42)
```

In this vignette, we use the template model "augm-infection-time" where surveys are conditioned on single introduction.
We load the parameter definitions directly from the model template.

```{r}
hhsimul <- new_housepi_model("augm-infection-time") |>
  load_parameter_template()

# inspect parameter definitions
hhsimul |> get_parameters()
```

## Infectivity Profile

To model transmission, 
In `housepi` we follow the convention for infectivity profiles to be function of the generation time.
Generation time is defined as the time from infection to transmission.

Certain profiles will then be conditioned on individuals incubation periods

| Delay                 | Infector Incub. Period | Infectee Incub. Period | Supported |
|-----------------------|:----------------------:|:----------------------:|:---------:|
| Generation Time       | &cross;                | &cross;                |  &check;  |
| Onset to Transmission | &check;                | &cross;                |  &check;  |
| Serial Time           | &check;                | &check;                |  &cross;  |

Imagine we would like to associate a gamma distribution as infectivity profile.
In this simple hypothesis all individuals will share the same profile which depends only on the generation time.
We can provide a custom infectivity profile calling `add_infec_profile()` as follows:

```{r}
hhsimul <- hhsimul |>
  add_infec_profile(name = "gamma", args = c(shape = 2.2, scale = 1.3))
```

Bear in mind that each model requiring an infectivity profile has a default profile.

## Simulate an Outbreak

We propose the following definitions for the augmented variables, 
associated from a list by calling `$load_augmented_list`.

```{r}
hhsimul <- hhsimul |>
  load_augmented_list(
    # define 'infec_time' as the difference between onset and incubation
    infec_time = "onset_time - incub_period",

    # define an 'onset_time' for each individual
    onset_time = list(
      model = "lnorm",
      args = c(meanlog = 4, sdlog = 0.5),
      max = 365
    ),

    # define an 'incub_period' for each individual
    incub_period = list(
      model = "gamma",
      # arguments of incubation period are linked to parameters
      args = c(shape = "inc_shape@P",  scale = "inc_scale@P"),
      max = 14
    )
  ) |>
  # append parameters for incubation period
  load_parameter_list(
    inc_shape = 2, inc_scale = 1.1, 
    append = TRUE
  )
```

We then run a simulation with the method `simulate`, using the same community structure from the survey, but dropping cases.
In this configuration, introductions are drawn randomly. 
Simulation will associated augmented incubation periods and onset times in addition to status.

```{r}
simulated <- hhsimul |> 
  add_dataset(housepi::survey |> dplyr::mutate(status = NA)) |>
  simulate()
head(simulated)
```

We then propose a simple observation process, where we assume onsets after 6 PM (18/24) are reported to next day.
Finally, we remove unobserved quantities:

```{r}
simulated <- simulated |>
  dplyr::mutate(onset_date = dplyr::if_else(
    status > 0, floor(onset_time) + ((onset_time %% 1) > 0.75), NA
  )) |>
  dplyr::select(-incub_period, -onset_time, -infec_time)
head(simulated)
```

## Validate the Simulation

We can check that inference returns the parameters used for the simulation.

```{r}
hhmodel <- hhsimul |>
  # drop previous augmented definitions
  drop_augmented() |> 
  # load definitions from list
  load_augmented_list(
    infec_time = "onset_time - incub_period",
    onset_time = list(
      rule = "norm", from = "onset_date@D", scale = 0.25
    ),
    incub_period = list(
      model = "gamma", 
      args = c(shape = "inc_shape@P", scale = "inc_scale@P")
    )
  ) |>
  # perform the inference
  infer(simulated, n_chains = 3, n_steps = 10000, n_adapt = 2000, 
        n_burnin = 1000, thin = 10, progress = 20)
```
We can visualize traces vs expected values as follows

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false
library(ggplot2)

# select parameters used for the simulation
simul_parameters <- hhsimul$parameters |> 
  dplyr::filter(!const) |>
  dplyr::select(name, value) |> 
  dplyr::rename(parameter = name, simulated = value)

# use bayesplot to plot the posterior draws
hhmodel |> 
  as_draws_df() |>
  bayesplot::mcmc_trace(facet_args = list(ncol = 1)) +
  geom_hline(data = simul_parameters, aes(yintercept = simulated),
             colour = "coral", linewidth = 1)
```

```{r}
#| fig.width: 5
#| fig.height: 2.5
# compute Rhat values associate to inferred parameters
traces <- hhmodel |> as_draws_df()
var_names <- hhmodel |> 
  get_parameters() |> 
  dplyr::filter(!const) |> 
  dplyr::pull(name)
rhat_values <- sapply(var_names, function(v) posterior::rhat(traces[[v]]))

# use bayesplot to showcase Rhat statistics
bayesplot::mcmc_rhat(rhat_values) + 
  bayesplot::yaxis_text(hjust = 1)
```

Here we performed R-hat diagnostics computing the values of $\hat{R}$ with [posterior](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/posterior/).

Finally we wrap all together to compare to parameters used for simulation.

```{r}
hhmodel |> as_draws_df() |> 
  posterior::summarise_draws() |>
  dplyr::reframe(parameter = variable,
                 inferred = sprintf("%0.4f [%0.4f, %0.4f]", mean, q5, q95)) |>
  dplyr::inner_join(simul_parameters, by = "parameter") |>
  flextable::flextable() |>
  flextable::separate_header() |>
  flextable::theme_vanilla() |>
  flextable::bold(j = ~ parameter, bold = TRUE) |> 
  flextable::bg(bg = "white", part = "all") |>
  flextable::autofit()
```
